title: Successful multidisciplinary management of massive cerebral hemorrhage at 19 weeks of gestation to full-term delivery: a case report.
abstract: Cerebral hemorrhage (ICH) during pregnancy is a rare but catastrophic event. Its occurrence in the early-to-mid second trimester without classic risk factors poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Here, we report a 33-year-old pregnant woman at 19 weeks of gestation with a history of tuberculous meningitis (requiring ventriculostomy) and in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer (IVF-ET), who developed a massive cerebral hemorrhage (>140 mL), intraventricular hemorrhage, and acute hydrocephalus. Notably, she had no hypertension or preeclampsia, but serological testing revealed positive anti-Ro-52 and anti-Scl-70 antibodies. Emergency neurosurgical interventions, including craniotomy, hematoma evacuation, and neuroendoscopic clot removal, were performed. This was followed by multidisciplinary management, incorporating hydroxychloroquine for immunomodulation and thromboprophylaxis. The patient achieved favorable neurological recovery and delivered a healthy infant at term without the need for permanent shunting. The uniqueness of this case lies in the concurrent presence of prior tuberculous meningitis, neurosurgical history, positive autoimmune serology, and assisted reproductive technology (ART). We propose a 'multiple-hit' hypothesis as a speculative, hypothesis-generating framework-rather than a proven pathogenic mechanism-involving chronic infection-induced vascular remodeling, autoimmune-mediated endothelial injury, and pregnancy-related immune dysregulation, which warrants further investigation in larger cohorts. This report raises the question of whether comprehensive autoimmune screening might be considered in pregnant patients with ICH of unknown etiology, although larger studies are needed to validate this approach. It also underscores the role of coordinated multidisciplinary care in the management of such complex cases, although its impact on outcomes remains to be determined.

title: Beyond the Lungs: A Case of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Without Pulmonary Involvement.
abstract: The coexistence of sarcoidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an uncommon but increasingly recognized phenomenon. Limited data exist regarding its epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and optimal management. We present the case of a 58-year-old female with a history of SLE who developed a chronic, relapsing annular rash affecting her arms and neck over three years. She also experienced frequent headaches with normal neuroimaging. Laboratory testing revealed positive antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), Cytoplasmic Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (C-ANCA) with Anti-Proteinase 3 (PR3) specificity, nucleosome antibodies. A skin biopsy subsequently led to a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Unlike most reported cases, which primarily feature pulmonary involvement, this patient exhibited no significant respiratory symptoms. The unusual presence of C-ANCA positivity, more commonly associated with vasculitis, raised the possibility of an overlap syndrome. She was successfully treated with corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine, resulting in clinical improvement. This case highlights the need to consider cutaneous sarcoidosis as a potential coexisting condition with SLE, particularly in the absence of pulmonary involvement. Increased awareness of atypical presentations may lead to earlier recognition and improved outcomes. Further research is warranted to better characterize the relationship between these two autoimmune conditions and to refine therapeutic strategies for patients with this rare coexistence.
journal: Journal of investigative medicine high impact case reports
